nodes.label: Rome
nodes.full: The empire Palmyra taxes trade on the edge of, is granted citizenship by in 212, defends when its emperor is captured in 260, breaks away from under Zenobia, and is razed by when Aurelian reconquers the East in 272–73.
nodes.src: background — Millar, 'The Roman Near East' (1993); Watson, 'Aurelian and the Third Century' (1999)

nodes.label: Sassanid Persia
nodes.full: The rival empire on the other side of the Euphrates — the market Palmyrene caravans reach at Spasinou Charax and Seleucia, and, under Shapur I, the power that captures Valerian in 260 and is then twice driven back to Ctesiphon by Odaenathus.
nodes.src: background — the Res Gestae Divi Saporis (ŠKZ); Zosimus 1.36–39

nodes.label: Palmyra as autonomous caravan city
nodes.full: For three centuries Palmyra operates as a semi-autonomous caravan city within the Roman sphere — taxing the Silk Road trade between Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean; its extraordinary wealth visible in the colonnaded streets, temples and tower tombs that survive today.
nodes.src: Palmyra's semi-autonomous status: Pliny, Natural History 5.88 ('Palmyra, a city famous for its situation, its wealth and its soil') — 1st c. CE. The city's self-governing institutions: Tariff inscription 137 CE (Hermitage) documents its own council (boule). PAT corpus (~3,000 inscriptions): Hillers & Cussini (1996). The grant of Roman citizenship under Caracalla 212 CE: marks the transition to the next phase.

nodes.label: Odaenathus I — first titled Palmyrene lord
nodes.full: The first Palmyrene ruler to bear the title 'Lord of Palmyra' in inscriptions — grandfather of the famous Odaenathus; his inscriptions establish the dynastic lineage that will produce the breakaway empire.
nodes.src: Inscription CIS II 3946: names Odaenathus as 'lord of Palmyra'. PAT corpus. Gawlikowski (1985) on the Palmyrene dynastic titulature. The grandfather-grandson name repetition is characteristic of Palmyrene aristocratic naming patterns.

nodes.label: Odaenathus II — defeats Shapur I, saves the Roman East
nodes.full: After Valerian's capture by Shapur I in 260, Odaenathus defeats the victorious Persian army twice and drives it back to Ctesiphon — single-handedly saving the Roman East; Gallienus grants him the title 'corrector totius Orientis' and he becomes the de facto ruler of the entire East.
nodes.src: Odaenathus's campaigns: Zosimus 1.39 (most detailed). SHA Vita Gallieni 10–12. Festus, Breviarium 23. His title 'corrector totius Orientis': documented in two Palmyrene inscriptions (CIS II 3971, 3946). The Persian defeat at Ctesiphon: Zosimus 1.39.2. Stoneman (1992), Palmyra and Its Empire: the standard modern study.

nodes.label: Zenobia — regent, conqueror, queen of the East
nodes.full: After Odaenathus's assassination, Zenobia rules as regent for her son Vaballathus — then conquers Egypt (269), Asia Minor and much of the Roman East (270–271); she proclaims herself and Vaballathus co-rulers, dropping Aurelian's name from coins; Aurelian defeats her at Emesa and Immae (272).
nodes.src: WELL DOCUMENTED: Zosimus 1.44–56 (most detailed). SHA Vita Aureliani 22–31 (hostile but detailed). Pollio, SHA Vita Zenobiae. Palmyrene coins of Vaballathus and Zenobia: RIC V Aurelian 381–390 shows the coinage sequence — Aurelian's name disappears, confirming the break. Watson (1999), Aurelian and the Third Century: the standard modern study.

nodes.label: Vaballathus — child emperor, last Palmyrene ruler
nodes.full: Son of Odaenathus and Zenobia — proclaimed 'Basileus Basileon' (King of Kings) on Palmyrene coins; his mother ruled in his name; defeated at Emesa and Immae in 272, paraded in Aurelian's triumph in Rome 274; the dynasty ends with him.
nodes.src: Vaballathus coins: RIC V Aurelian 381–390 — the sequence showing first joint coinage with Aurelian, then Vaballathus alone as Augustus is the primary documentary evidence for the breakaway. SHA Vita Aureliani 28–31. The triumph in Rome 274: SHA Vita Aureliani 33–34. Watson (1999) pp.68–91.

nodes.label: Odaenathus defeats Shapur I — Persian army routed
nodes.full: Odaenathus launches two campaigns against Shapur I after the capture of Valerian — defeats the Persian army retreating from Roman territory and twice besieges Ctesiphon; the most successful military response to the Persian crisis of 260.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.39 (most detailed). SHA Vita Gallieni 10.1–7. Festus, Breviarium 23. The Res Gestae Divi Saporis (ŠKZ) does NOT mention these defeats — notable omission. Odaenathus's campaigns: confirmed in multiple sources but dates debated (260–263). Stoneman (1992) pp.108–127.

nodes.label: Zenobia conquers Egypt — Timagenes expelled
nodes.full: Zenobia sends her general Zabdas with 70,000 troops to conquer Egypt — the Roman prefect Tenagino Probus is defeated and killed; Egypt, Rome's grain supply, falls to Palmyra in a single campaign.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.44 (most detailed; names Zabdas and 70,000 troops). SHA Vita Aureliani 22. Egypt papyri: some papyri from 270–272 CE date by Vaballathus's regnal years rather than Roman emperors — confirming Palmyrene control. Thomas (1976), 'The Date of the Revolt of L. Domitius Domitianus' in ZPE 22.

nodes.label: Zenobia conquers Asia Minor and Arabia
nodes.full: Zenobia's forces advance to Ancyra (mod. Ankara) in the north and control Arabia in the south — at the peak of Palmyrene power the empire controls Egypt, the Levant and much of Asia Minor; larger than the Roman East.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.50 (advance to Ancyra). SHA Vita Aureliani 22.1. The extent of Palmyrene control: confirmed in papyri from Egypt and inscriptions from Asia Minor. Millar (1993), The Roman Near East pp.169–173. Stoneman (1992) pp.155–165 maps the maximum extent.

nodes.label: Battle of Immae — Aurelian defeats Zenobia
nodes.full: Aurelian defeats the Palmyrene heavy cavalry at Immae by feigning retreat to exhaust the armoured horses, then counter-attacking — the decisive tactical move documented in detail by Zosimus; followed by the Battle of Emesa and the siege of Palmyra itself.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.50–52 (detailed tactical account — feigned retreat vs. heavy cavalry). SHA Vita Aureliani 25. The tactical detail is unusually precise for a late antique battle account: Zosimus 1.50.3–4. Watson (1999) pp.68–83. The Emesa battle follows immediately: Zosimus 1.52.

nodes.label: Fall of Palmyra — city sacked, then razed
nodes.full: Aurelian besieges and takes Palmyra in 272, then after a second revolt in 273 returns and orders the city razed — the end of Palmyra as a major city; the archaeological destruction layer is visible in the ruins today.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.54–56. SHA Vita Aureliani 26–31. The second sack 273: SHA Vita Aureliani 31. The destruction layer: visible at the Temple of Bel and other excavated sites. Gawlikowski (1974), Palmyre VI: archaeological evidence for the sack. Watson (1999) pp.84–91.

nodes.label: Palmyrene Tariff inscription of 137 CE
nodes.full: The most detailed ancient price document outside Diocletian's Edict — lists taxes on hundreds of goods passing through Palmyra, from purple-dyed fleeces to prostitutes; both Greek and Palmyrene Aramaic versions survive, giving the city's own bilingual administrative record.
nodes.src: HARD ANCHOR: Tariff inscription 137 CE — stone slab, partially in situ at Palmyra; fragments in Hermitage Museum (inv. 3923). First published Sachau (1881). Matthews (1984), The Tax Law of Palmyra, JRS 74: the standard modern study. The document lists: salt fish, bronze vessels, olive oil, pine nuts, dried fruit, wool, slaves, prostitutes — 'for each prostitute, one denarius per act.' The bilingual format (Greek administrative, Palmyrene fiscal) is unique.

nodes.label: Palmyrene city constitution — the boule and strategos
nodes.full: Palmyra governs itself through a Hellenistic-style city council (boule) alongside its own tribal structure — the inscriptions document both systems operating simultaneously; the city is both a polis and a tribal entity.
nodes.src: PAT corpus inscriptions: multiple boule references. Millar (1993), The Roman Near East pp.319–336 on Palmyrene self-government. The dual Greek-Palmyrene administration: Teixidor (1984), Un port romain du désert. The boule membership: documented in dedicatory inscriptions at the Palmyra Museum.

nodes.label: Zenobia's religious tolerance — Jews, Christians, Manichaeans
nodes.full: Zenobia's court is notably tolerant — she protects Paul of Samosata (bishop of Antioch, expelled by Church councils), employs the Neoplatonist philosopher Longinus as her chief advisor, and is sympathetically described by Jewish sources; her court is the most religiously diverse of the 3rd century.
nodes.src: Paul of Samosata: Eusebius, HE 7.27–30 (Zenobia's protection of the deposed bishop). Longinus as advisor: Zosimus 1.56.2; Porphyry, Vita Plotini 21. Jewish sources: multiple Talmudic passages treat Zenobia favourably. The religious diversity of the court: Millar (1993), Roman Near East pp.174–177. Watson (1999) pp.60–67.

nodes.label: Temple of Bel — the supreme Palmyrene sanctuary
nodes.full: The Temple of Bel at Palmyra is dedicated in 32 CE — its Greek and Palmyrene bilingual dedication inscription survives; Bel is a Babylonian import syncretised with the local triad (Bel, Yarhibol, Aglibol); the temple's cella survived until 2015 when ISIS partially destroyed it.
nodes.src: HARD ANCHOR: Dedication inscription 32 CE (bilingual Greek-Palmyrene): in situ and published (CIS II 3914). Teixidor (1979), The Pagan God pp.25–45 on the Bel triad. The temple: partially extant; Seyrig (1940–50) excavation reports. The solar triad Bel-Yarhibol-Aglibol: documented in hundreds of votive inscriptions. Gawlikowski (1973), Le Temple Palmyrénien.

nodes.label: Allat at Palmyra — goddess as Athena
nodes.full: Allat is worshipped at Palmyra as 'Allat-Athena' — her colossal cult statue (now fragmentary) equates the Arabian goddess with the Greek deity; the goddess's bilingual inscriptions document the syncretic religious world of the Palmyrene merchant class.
nodes.src: Temple of Allat: excavated 1975 (Gawlikowski 1977). The Allat-Athena statue: National Museum of Damascus (now fragmentary). CIS II inscriptions: multiple Allat dedications. Teixidor (1979), The Pagan God pp.53–60. The syncretism: Baalshamin and Aglibol also appear; the pantheon reflects Palmyra's position at the junction of Arabian, Mesopotamian and Hellenistic traditions.

nodes.label: Paul of Samosata — bishop of Antioch under Zenobia's protection
nodes.full: Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, teaches a low Christology (Christ as a man elevated to divine status) that Church councils condemn — Zenobia protects him from expulsion; when Aurelian defeats Zenobia he expels Paul, with the Roman emperor now enforcing Church decisions.
nodes.src: Eusebius, HE 7.27–30 (primary source; contemporary). The Council of Antioch 268 CE that condemned Paul: documented in HE 7.29. Aurelian's expulsion of Paul 272: Eusebius HE 7.30.19 — Aurelian sides with the Roman bishops, the first imperial enforcement of Church orthodoxy. Lane Fox (1986), Pagans and Christians pp.566–573.

nodes.label: Palmyrene tower tombs — the valley of the dead
nodes.full: Multi-storey tower tombs rising up to 22m line the roads entering Palmyra — each holds a wealthy family's dead across generations; their dated foundation inscriptions span 300 years, making the tower tomb sequence the most precisely dated architectural corpus in the Syrian desert.
nodes.src: Extant (Valley of the Tombs, Palmyra). Inscribed foundation dates: spanning 1st c. BC to 3rd c. CE. Gawlikowski (1970), Monuments funéraires de Palmyre: the standard study. The dated inscriptions: PAT corpus. The towers' social function: Yon (2002), Les notables de Palmyre. ISIS damaged several towers in 2015.

nodes.label: Palmyrene funerary busts — the portrait tradition
nodes.full: Hundreds of limestone funerary portrait busts from Palmyrene tombs survive — they are among the most vivid portrait sculpture of the Roman world, showing jewellery, dress and facial features of the Palmyrene merchant class; they are the primary evidence for Palmyrene material culture.
nodes.src: Major collections: National Museum of Damascus, Louvre, British Museum, NY Carlsberg Glyptotek. Smith (2013), The Sculptor's Eye: the standard iconographic study. Over 300 busts published. The jewellery depicted: Higgins (1980) identifies specific types paralleled in Roman Syrian contexts. The dated examples: inscribed with the deceased's name and date in Palmyrene Aramaic.

nodes.label: Colonnaded street of Palmyra — monumental urban space
nodes.full: A 1.2km colonnaded street runs through the centre of Palmyra with over 200 columns, many bearing consoles that once held portrait statues of prominent citizens — the most complete example of Roman-era urban monumentalism outside Rome itself.
nodes.src: Extant (Palmyra). Consoles with inscriptions: Yon (2002), Les notables de Palmyre catalogues all portrait inscriptions from the columns. The street's construction phasing: documented in building inscriptions (PAT). The citizen portrait programme: unique in the Roman world for its density and extent. Seyrig (1950) on the urban development.

nodes.label: Palmyrene coinage under Vaballathus and Zenobia
nodes.full: The Palmyrene coinage sequence is the primary documentary evidence for the breakaway: first Vaballathus and Aurelian on equal coins, then Vaballathus alone as Augustus with Zenobia as Augusta — the moment Aurelian's name disappears marks the formal break.
nodes.src: RIC V Aurelian 381–390: the full sequence documented. The coins struck at Antioch under Palmyrene control: confirmed by mint marks. Watson (1999), Aurelian and the Third Century pp.61–68 analyses the numismatic sequence as political document. The Zenobia-Augusta coins: first woman on Roman imperial coinage as a ruling authority (not consort).

nodes.label: Palmyrene banquet reliefs — music at the symposium
nodes.full: Funerary banquet reliefs from Palmyrene tomb chambers depict reclining figures with musicians playing the kithara and aulos — the primary evidence for musical performance in Palmyrene elite culture, embedded in the funerary feast tradition that bridges Greek symposium and local practice.
nodes.src: Banquet reliefs: multiple examples in National Museum of Damascus and international collections. Dentzer (1982), Le motif du banquet couché dans le Proche-Orient et le monde grec: catalogues the Palmyrene examples. The instruments depicted: kithara (Greek lyre) and aulos (double pipe). The fusion of Greek symposium iconography with Palmyrene dress and jewellery is characteristic of the city's cultural hybridity.

nodes.label: Longinus — Neoplatonist philosopher at Zenobia's court
nodes.full: Cassius Longinus is the greatest literary critic and philosopher of the 3rd century — Zenobia appoints him chief secretary and advisor; when Aurelian captures Palmyra he executes Longinus specifically, recognising him as the intellectual architect of Zenobia's independence.
nodes.src: Porphyry, Vita Plotini 14, 19–20 (contemporary; Longinus as philosopher). His role at Zenobia's court: Zosimus 1.56.2. His execution: Zosimus 1.56.2 and SHA Vita Aureliani 30.3. The treatise 'On the Sublime' (Peri Hypsous): attributed to 'Longinus' though authorship debated. Millar (1993), Roman Near East pp.174–175.

nodes.label: Zosimus — principal source, with limitations
nodes.full: Zosimus's New History is the most detailed surviving account of Odaenathus, Zenobia and Aurelian's reconquest — written 200 years after the events, using earlier lost sources; his account of the Battle of Immae's tactical detail suggests access to a contemporary military narrative.
nodes.src: Zosimus, Historia Nova 1.38–56: covers the Palmyrene period. The 200-year gap: Zosimus draws on Dexippus (3rd c., lost) and other sources. The Battle of Immae account (1.50): its tactical specificity suggests a near-contemporary source. Ridley (1982), Zosimus: New History (translation with notes). Watson (1999) pp.1–22 on the sources.

nodes.label: PAT corpus — 3,000 Palmyrene inscriptions
nodes.full: The Palmyrene Aramaic Text corpus (~3,000 inscriptions) is the primary source base for the city — it includes dedicatory, funerary, honorific and commercial texts in Palmyrene Aramaic and bilingual Greek; together they reconstruct the city's social, commercial and religious life.
nodes.src: PAT: Hillers & Cussini (1996), Palmyrene Aramaic Texts (Johns Hopkins University Press) — the standard corpus. The bilingual inscriptions: Yon (2002), Les notables de Palmyre — the honorific statue bases. The commercial texts: primarily the Tariff inscription (o1). The funerary inscriptions: Gawlikowski (1970). Major collections: National Museum Damascus, Louvre, British Museum, Hermitage.

nodes.label: Silk Road control — Palmyra as the key node
nodes.full: Palmyra sits at the junction of the routes from Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean — its caravan trade taxes fund the city's extraordinary building programme; Palmyrene merchants operate from Dacia to India.
nodes.src: Pliny, Natural History 5.88: 'Palmyra, famous for its wealth.' Strabo 16.1.27 on the route. Palmyrene merchant inscriptions from Dura-Europos, Spasinou Charax (Persian Gulf) and Seleucia: PAT corpus. Young (2001), Rome's Eastern Trade pp.165–190. The Tariff inscription (o1): documents the goods taxed.

nodes.label: Palmyrene merchants across the Roman world
nodes.full: Palmyrene merchant inscriptions are found from Britain to India — a Palmyrene temple inscription from South Shields (Arbeia) on Hadrian's Wall, Palmyrene traders at Dacia, Palmyrene gods worshipped in Rome; the most widely distributed merchant community in the Roman Empire.
nodes.src: South Shields (Arbeia) altar: 'To the goddess Hamia, Barates the Palmyrene erected this' (RIB 1.1075) — extant, South Shields Museum. Dacia Palmyrene inscriptions: multiple (IDR III). Palmyrene temple in Rome: CIL VI.710. Dirven (1999), The Palmyrenes of Dura-Europos. The geographical distribution: Teixidor (1984), Un port romain du désert ch.3.

nodes.label: Palmyrene trade network — Rome to Parthia
nodes.full: Palmyrene caravans operate beyond the Roman frontier into Parthian/Sassanid territory — Palmyrene merchant inscriptions from Seleucia-on-Tigris and Spasinou Charax (Persian Gulf) document trade routes that cross two empires; Palmyra is the only city embedded in both.
nodes.src: Spasinou Charax inscription: PAT 0263 — Palmyrene merchant at the head of the Persian Gulf. Seleucia inscription: PAT 0277. Young (2001), Rome's Eastern Trade pp.165–200. The crossing of imperial boundaries: legally complex — documented in the Tariff inscription's provisions for goods entering from Parthian territory.

nodes.label: Palmyrene art — Greek, Parthian and Arabian fusion
nodes.full: Palmyrene art fuses Greek (figural composition, architectural orders), Parthian (frontal poses, carpet-patterned garments) and Arabian (goddess types, camel imagery) traditions — the result is a distinctive hybrid visual culture found nowhere else in the ancient world.
nodes.src: The frontality in Palmyrene sculpture: Colledge (1976), The Art of Palmyra — the standard study. The Parthian influence: frontality as a Parthian convention adapted into Palmyrene funerary portraits. Greek architectural orders at the Temple of Bel: Browning (1979), Palmyra. The Arabian elements: Teixidor (1979), The Pagan God pp.25–55. The synthesis is most visible in the funerary busts (a2).

nodes.label: Odaenathus's Roman titles and Palmyrene ambiguity
nodes.full: Odaenathus holds simultaneously Roman titles (corrector totius Orientis, consul) and Palmyrene titles ('King of Kings' — retrospectively) — the ambiguity is documented; Rome and Palmyra each read his status differently, and this interpretive gap is what Zenobia exploits.
nodes.src: Roman titles: documented in Latin inscriptions (CIL III). Palmyrene titles: CIS II 3971 — 'king of kings' appears in Palmyrene but not in Latin versions of his titles. The interpretive gap: Millar (1993), Roman Near East pp.170–173 analyses the difference between Roman and Palmyrene titulature carefully. Watson (1999) pp.39–55.

nodes.label: The crisis of 260 — Palmyra fills the Roman vacuum
nodes.full: The capture of Valerian in 260 leaves the Roman East leaderless — Odaenathus fills the vacuum not by rebellion but by defending Roman territory; his success makes Palmyra indispensable and gives it the military prestige Zenobia will convert into imperial ambition.
nodes.src: Valerian's capture: Res Gestae Divi Saporis (ŠKZ), Ka'ba-ye Zardosht (Sassanid inscription — primary source). Zosimus 1.36 on the aftermath. The vacuum Odaenathus fills: Potter (1990), Prophecy and History in the Crisis of the Roman Empire pp.371–380. Watson (1999) pp.30–42.

nodes.label: Aurelian reunifies the empire — Palmyra as turning point
nodes.full: Aurelian's defeat of Zenobia (272) and the Gallic Empire (274) reunifies Rome — Palmyra's destruction is the pivotal event; the empire that emerges is more centralised, more militarised and on the path to Diocletian's tetrarchy.
nodes.src: Watson (1999), Aurelian and the Third Century: the standard study. The reunification 272–274: Zosimus 1.50–62. SHA Vita Aureliani 22–37. The consequences for Roman administrative history: Rees (2004), Diocletian and the Tetrarchy ch.1. Aurelian's coinage reform 274: also a consequence of Palmyrene disruption of eastern mints.

nodes.label: Zenobia — the most documented pre-Islamic Arab woman
nodes.full: Zenobia is the most extensively documented woman in pre-Islamic Near Eastern history — she commands armies, conducts diplomacy, patronises philosophy, claims descent from Cleopatra, and debates her own captors; the SHA dedicates an entire biography to her (Vita Zenobiae), unique for a non-Roman woman.
nodes.src: SHA Vita Zenobiae (Historia Augusta): a full biographical entry — unique for a non-Roman woman. Zosimus 1.44–56 (most detailed on the campaigns). The Cleopatra descent claim: SHA Vita Zenobiae 1.2. Stoneman (1992), Palmyra and Its Empire ch.8–12. Southern (2008), Empress Zenobia: Palmyra's Rebel Queen: the standard modern biography. Her fate after capture: debated — sources give marriage to a Roman senator, death on the march, or suicide.

nodes.label: Palmyrene women in inscription evidence
nodes.full: Palmyrene funerary inscriptions name women as tomb owners and dedicants; a small number of honorific inscriptions record women receiving public statues — Aqmat daughter of Maliku is named on a consol inscription at the Grand Colonnade, one of the very few women in the Palmyrene civic honorific record.
nodes.src: Yon (2002), Les notables de Palmyre: documents all honorific inscriptions including female subjects. The Aqmat inscription: PAT 1347. Funerary inscriptions naming women: multiple in PAT corpus (Gawlikowski 1970). The pattern: women are documented in funerary contexts more than civic — the civic inscriptions are dominated by male caravan merchants. Matthews (1984) on women in Palmyrene commercial contexts.

nodes.label: Palmyrene slave trade — documented in the Tariff
nodes.full: The Palmyrene Tariff of 137 CE includes a tax on enslaved persons passing through the city — enslaved people are listed alongside bronze vessels and olive oil as taxable commercial goods; the single most direct ancient Near Eastern documentation of the slave trade as a fiscal category.
nodes.src: Tariff inscription 137 CE (Hermitage; Matthews 1984): the enslaved persons tax rate. The Tariff lists enslaved persons under 'imported goods' — fiscally equivalent to commodities. Matthews (1984), The Tax Law of Palmyra, JRS 74 pp.165–166 on the slavery provisions. The document is a CATEGORICAL SHIFT entry: it shows the Roman-era fiscal categorisation of persons as property in a primary administrative document.
